paragraphs: §1 — The claim to be refuted: the promised temple and the messianic tidings are already past

[The claim is] that the promised temple whose building יְחֶזְקֵאל and others mentioned has [already] passed and been carried out, and that it is the temple that was built a second time, mentioned in עֶזְרָא; and likewise that all the good tidings (al-bishārāt) with which יְשַׁעְיָה and יִרְמְיָהוּ (peace be upon them) and others gave glad tidings — those that are to be in the days of the Messiah — have [already] been and have run their course.

: §1 states only the position to be demolished; Q gives no preamble of method here because the method was set in Bab 23 (the bab "that precedes this one," to which Bab 23's tail explicitly cross-refers). The position is double-fronted: it is the Christian "the Messiah has already come, the prophecies are fulfilled" claim (continuous with Bab 14's "Ezekiel's temple was the Second Temple"), but Q's primary target in this run (Babs 21–24) is the intra-Jewish version held by the Daniel al-Qūmisī circle — the Jews whom Q at §9 calls "a people of those firm in the religion" who "shared with [the Christians] in that." al-bishārāt (the "good tidings/glad announcements" of the prophets) is the technical pivot-word of the whole bab; al-ajal ("the appointed time"), used throughout §§3–6 as shorthand, denotes the redemptive/messianic era whose prophecies are at issue.
§2 — Righteousness and joy promised, but Ezra-Nehemiah record sin and remnant-misery

Among that which gives the lie to their claim in this [matter] is the saying of יְשַׁעְיָהוּ (peace be upon him) concerning the appointed time [Isa 60:21] וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים לְעוֹלָם יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ ("and your people shall all be righteous; they shall inherit the land forever") — while [Ezra] says, after the building of the Second Temple, in עֶזְרָא [Ezra 10:2] אֲנַחְנוּ מָעַלְנוּ בֵאלֹהֵינוּ ("we have trespassed against our God"), together with the rest of what is mentioned there of the affair of נְחֶמְיָה [Neh 12:43] וַתִּשָּׁמַע שִׂמְחַת יְרוּשָׁלִַם etc., and likewise the affair of [Neh 13:15-22] דֹּרְכִים גִּתּוֹת בַּשַּׁבָּת ("treading winepresses on the Sabbath"). So what is plainer than this?

And he says, among the tidings to come [Ezek 34:29] לֹא יִהְיוּ עוֹד אֲסֻפֵי רָעָב וְלֹא יִשְׂאוּ עוֹד כְּלִמַּת etc. ("they shall no more be consumed by hunger, nor bear the reproach [of the nations]"); and he says [Isa 54:4] וְחֶרְפַּת אַלְמְנוּתַיִךְ לֹא תִזְכְּרִי עוֹד ("and the reproach of your widowhood you shall remember no more"); and he says [Isa 61:7] תַּחַת בָּשְׁתְּכֶם מִשְׁנֶה וּכְלִמָּה יָרֹנּוּ חֶלְקָם ("instead of your shame [you shall have] a double portion"); and he says [Isa 61:9] וְנוֹדַע בַּגּוֹיִם זַרְעָם etc. ("their seed shall be known among the nations"). Yet he says, in the affair of עֶזְרָא (peace be upon him), the contrary of that — namely his saying [Neh 1:3] הַנִּשְׁאָרִים אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁאֲרוּ מִן הַשְּׁבִי שָׁם בַּמְּדִינָה בְּרָעָה גְדֹלָה וּבְחֶרְפָּה etc. ("the remnant that survived the captivity, there in the province, in great trouble and reproach").

: The structural engine of §§2–6: a taqābul (matched-opposition) catalogue. Each redemptive promise from Isaiah/Ezekiel/Jeremiah/Zechariah is paired with an explicit notice in Ezra-Nehemiah that the post-Exilic community was in the opposite condition. If the Second Temple era were the promised redemption, these contraries could not stand on record. The argument is purely from Scripture's internal consistency (the same al-kitāb lā yajūz ʿalayhi al-tanāquḍ axiom Q wields throughout the Maqala): the promises and their documented non-fulfilment cannot both describe the same period, so the redemption must be still future. Note Q's marginal pointer to "Neh 12:43" + "Neh 13:15" is given by incipit only ("וַתִּשָּׁמַע … דֹּרְכִים גִּתּוֹת בַּשַּׁבָּת"), the Sabbath-profanation of Neh 13 being adduced as proof that the post-Exilic community was not the all-righteous people of Isa 60:21.
§3 — Dominion over the nations and the throwing-off of the yoke promised, but Nehemiah records bondage

And he says, among the tidings for the appointed time [Isa 60:12] כִּי הַגּוֹי וְהַמַּמְלָכָה אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַעַבְדוּךְ יֹאבֵדוּ etc. ("for the nation and kingdom that will not serve you shall perish"); and he says [Isa 49:23] וְהָיוּ מְלָכִים אֹמְנַיִךְ וְשָׂרוֹתֵיהֶם מֵינִיקֹתַיִךְ אַפַּיִם אֶרֶץ יִשְׁתַּחֲווּ לָךְ וַעֲפַר רַגְלַיִךְ יְלַחֵכוּ ("and kings shall be your foster-fathers … they shall bow to you with their faces to the earth and lick the dust of your feet"); and he says [Nah 1:13] וְעַתָּה אֶשְׁבֹּר מֹטֵהוּ מֵעָלַיִךְ etc. ("and now I will break his yoke-bar from upon you"); [and] in [Jer 30:8] וְהָיָה בַיּוֹם הַהוּא נְאֻם [יְיָ] אֶשְׁבֹּר עֻלּוֹ מֵעַל צַוָּארֶךָ etc. ("on that day, says the Lord, I will break his yoke from upon your neck"); and he says [Jer 30:9] וְלֹא יַעַבְדוּ בּוֹ עוֹד ("and they shall serve [foreigners] no more"). And the contrary of that [is] in what is past: נְחֶמְיָה [Neh 9:36] הִנֵּה אֲנַחְנוּ הַיּוֹם עֲבָדִים etc. ("behold, we are slaves this day"), [and Neh 9:36-37] כֹּבְשִׁים and הִנֵּה אֲנַחְנוּ כַעֲבָדִים [וְ]אֶת בָּנֵינוּ וְאֶת בְּנוֹתֵינוּ etc. ("[over our bodies they rule] … and behold, we [are] as slaves, and our sons and our daughters").

: The second pair: the imperial promises (the nations serving Israel, the breaking of the foreign yoke — Isa 60:12, 49:23; Nah 1:13; Jer 30:8-9) against Neh 9:36-37, where the returnees confess "we are slaves this day" in their own land, paying tribute to foreign kings. The Nahum and Jeremiah "I will break his yoke" verses are the precise antitheses of Nehemiah's "we are slaves." The OCR for the Nahum citation was badly corrupted (the diff-report shows the Kraken pass produced near-gibberish); the multimodal reading וְעַתָּה אֶשְׁבֹּר מֹטֵהוּ מֵעָלַיִךְ restores Nah 1:13 cleanly, and Q's marginal בנחום א ("in Nahum 1") confirms it.
§4 — Perpetually open gates and the in-gathering promised, but Nehemiah keeps the gates shut

And he says, concerning the appointed time, in יְשַׁעְיָה [Isa 60:11] וּפִתְּחוּ שְׁעָרַיִךְ תָּמִיד יוֹמָם וָלַיְלָה לֹא יִסָּגֵרוּ etc. ("and your gates shall be open continually, day and night they shall not be shut"); and the contrary of that [is] in what is past, in נְחֶמְיָה [Neh 7:3] לֹא יִפָּתְחוּ שַׁעֲרֵי יְרוּשָׁלַם עַד חֹם הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ etc. ("let not the gates of Jerusalem be opened until the sun is hot"). And he says, concerning the appointed time, in זְכַרְיָה [Zech 8:7] הִנְנִי מוֹשִׁיעַ אֶת עַמִּי מֵאֶרֶץ מִזְרָח etc. ("behold, I will save my people from the land of the east"); in יְשַׁעְיָה [Isa 11:12] וּנְפוּצוֹת יְהוּדָה יְקַבֵּץ מֵאַרְבַּע כַּנְפוֹת הָאָרֶץ ("and the dispersed of Judah he will gather from the four corners of the earth"); and also in [Ps 107:3] וּמֵאֲרָצוֹת קִבְּצָם מִמִּזְרָח וּמִמַּעֲרָב מִצָּפוֹן וּמִיָּם הִנְנִי מֵבִיא אוֹתָם מֵאֶרֶץ צָפוֹן ("and from the lands he gathered them, from east and from west, from north and from the sea") — whereas those who went up in the first return went up only from בָּבֶל alone.

: Two more pairs. (a) The eternally-open gates of redeemed Zion (Isa 60:11) versus Nehemiah's standing security order to keep the gates barred until full daylight (Neh 7:3) — a city under siege-conditions is not the city of the unfailing promise. (b) The universal in-gathering "from the four corners of the earth / from east and west and north and sea" (Isa 11:12; Ps 107:3, with Zech 8:7) versus the historical fact that the first return under Cyrus brought back only the Babylonian golah — "from בָּבֶל alone." Q's clinching observation that the return was geographically partial is an empirical-historical, not merely exegetical, point. (The closing הִנְנִי מֵבִיא אוֹתָם מֵאֶרֶץ צָפוֹן appears to be Q conflating Jer 31:7 / 16:15 phrasing into the Ps 107 citation; he runs the in-gathering verses as a single florilegium.)
§5 — Vast multiplication and universal pure speech promised, but Nehemiah records a scant people who cannot speak Judahite

And he says, concerning the appointed time, in יְשַׁעְיָה [Isa 49:21] וְאָמַרְתְּ בִּלְבָבֵךְ מִי יָלַד לִי אֶת אֵלֶּה וַאֲנִי שְׁכוּלָה etc. ("and you shall say in your heart, who bore me these, when I was bereaved"); like [Hos 2:1] וְהָיָה מִסְפַּר בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּחוֹל הַיָּם etc. ("and the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea"); [and] in יְחֶזְקֵאל [Ezek 36:38] כְּצֹאן קָדָשִׁים כְּצֹאן יְרוּשָׁלַם בְּמוֹעֲדֶיהָ etc. ("like the holy flock, like the flock of Jerusalem at her appointed feasts"). And the contrary of that [is] in what is past, in נְחֶמְיָה [Neh 7:4] וְהָעָם מְעַט בְּתוֹכָהּ etc. ("and the people within it were few"). And he says, concerning the appointed time, in צְפַנְיָה [Zeph 3:9] כִּי אָז אֶהְפֹּךְ אֶל עַמִּים שָׂפָה בְרוּרָה etc. ("for then I will turn to the peoples a pure speech"); [and] in זְכַרְיָה [Zech 14:9] וְהָיָה יְיָ לְמֶלֶךְ עַל כָּל הָאָרֶץ בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא יִהְיֶה יְיָ אֶחָד וּשְׁמוֹ אֶחָד ("and the Lord shall be king over all the earth; on that day the Lord shall be one and his name one"). And he said the contrary of that, in what is past, in נְחֶמְיָה [Neh 13:24] וְאֵינָם מַכִּירִים לְדַבֵּר יְהוּדִית etc. ("and they could not speak Judahite").

: Two further pairs. (a) The promised numerical explosion of Israel "as the sand of the sea" (Isa 49:21; Hos 2:1; Ezek 36:38) versus Neh 7:4, "the people within it were few." (b) The eschatological universal turning-to-pure-speech and recognition of the one God (Zeph 3:9; Zech 14:9) versus Neh 13:24, where the returnees' own children "could not speak Judahite" (the language assimilation Nehemiah deplores) — the opposite of a world brought to one pure tongue. The taqābul is exact: a redemption that universalizes pure speech cannot be the era in which even Jerusalem's children have lost Hebrew.
§6 — No oppressor and a native ruler promised, but Nehemiah records oppressive governors and tribute

And he says, concerning the appointed time, in זְכַרְיָה [Zech 9:8] וְלֹא יַעֲבֹר עֲלֵיהֶם עוֹד נֹגֵשׂ ("and no oppressor shall pass over them again"); in יִרְמְיָה [Jer 30:21] וְהָיָה אַדִּירוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ וּמֹשְׁלוֹ מִקִּרְבּוֹ יֵצֵא etc. ("and their prince shall be of themselves, and their ruler shall come forth from their midst"); in זְכַרְיָה [Zech 10:4] מִמֶּנּוּ יָצָא פִנָּה מִמֶּנּוּ יָצָא … מִמֶּנּוּ כָל נוֹגֵשׂ יַחְדָּו ("from him the corner-stone, from him … from him every ruler together"). And in what is past he said, in נְחֶמְיָה [Neh 5:15] וְהַפַּחוֹת הָרִאשֹׁנִים אֲשֶׁר לְפָנַי הִכְבִּידוּ עַל הָעָם etc. ("and the former governors who were before me laid heavy [burdens] upon the people"). And he says, concerning the appointed time, in יְשַׁעְיָה [Isa 62:8] אִם אֶתֵּן אֶת דְּגָנֵךְ עוֹד מַאֲכָל לְאֹיְבַיִךְ … כִּי מְאַסְפָיו יֹאכְלֻהוּ ("if I will give your grain again as food to your enemies … but they that gathered it shall eat it"); and in what is past he said, in נְחֶמְיָה [Neh 9:37] וּתְבוּאָתָהּ מַרְבָּה לַמְּלָכִים אֲשֶׁר נָתַתָּה עָלֵינוּ בְּחַטֹּאותֵינוּ etc. ("and its increase it yields in abundance to the kings you have set over us because of our sins").

: The last pair of the catalogue: (a) no oppressor and a self-sprung native ruler (Zech 9:8, 10:4; Jer 30:21) versus Nehemiah's "former governors laid heavy burdens" (Neh 5:15) — foreign and oppressive rule, not native sovereignty. (b) The promise that Israel's own harvest will no longer feed her enemies (Isa 62:8) versus Neh 9:37, where the produce of the land goes "to the kings you have set over us because of our sins." With this Q closes the Ezra-Nehemiah taqābul series; from §7 he turns from "promise vs. its past contrary" to "promise vs. its non-occurrence at all."
§7 — The Messiah's promised conquest never befell Jesus, nor the failed sectarian "messiahs"

And he says concerning the Messiah, in יְשַׁעְיָה [Isa 11:4] וְהִכָּה אֶרֶץ בְּשֵׁבֶט פִּיו etc. ("and he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth") — and this is the contrary of [what befell] Jesus, who met with being killed; and likewise Abū ʿĪsā, who fled and hid himself in the mountain; and likewise Yūdghān —

: Q here pivots from the Christian to the Jewish-sectarian false messiahs, lining them up as joint counter-examples to Isa 11:4's conquering Messiah: (1) Jesus, "killed and crucified" (the recurring refrain of Bab 6 §6 — the imperial-Messiah verses manifestly never applied to him); (2) Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī (the 8th-c. messianic claimant who, in Q's account in the sect-chapter of Maqala I, fled and was killed/hidden in battle); and (3) Yūdghān (Yūdghān al-Hamadhānī, the "Shepherd," whose followers, the Yūdghāniyya, claimed he had not died and would return). The sentence runs without a section break into §8 across the p164/p165 fold — the predicate ("…and likewise Yūdghān, who perished — these whose followers claimed their messiahship") completes at the top of §8.
§8 — These supposed messiahs perished; whereas Isaiah's tidings and Amos's and Obadiah's are unfulfilled

— [Yūdghān] who perished — these, whose followers claimed their messiahship. יְשַׁעְיָהוּ (peace be upon him) said [Isa 49:7] כֹּה אָמַר יְיָ גֹּאֵל יִשְׂרָאֵל קְדוֹשׁוֹ לִבְזֹה נֶפֶשׁ לִמְתָעֵב גּוֹי לְעֶבֶד מֹשְׁלִים מְלָכִים יִרְאוּ וְקָמוּ etc. ("thus says the Lord, the Redeemer of Israel, his Holy One, to him whom man despises … kings shall see and arise"), and he said [Isa 49:9] לֵאמֹר לַאֲסוּרִים צֵאוּ etc. ("saying to the prisoners, go forth"), [Isa 49:10] לֹא יִרְעָבוּ וְלֹא יִצְמָאוּ etc. ("they shall not hunger nor thirst"), [Isa 60:1] קוּמִי אוֹרִי כִּי בָא אוֹרֵךְ etc. ("arise, shine, for your light has come"); and זְכַרְיָה [9:10] וּמָשְׁלוֹ מִיָּם עַד יָם ("and his dominion shall be from sea to sea"); and דָּנִיֵּאל says [Dan 2:44] וּבְיוֹמֵיהוֹן דִּי מַלְכַיָּא אִנּוּן יְקִים אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא מַלְכוּ דִּי לְעָלְמִין לָא תִתְחַבַּל etc. ("and in the days of those kings the God of heaven shall set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed"). So can anyone say that any of these promises ever was [fulfilled], save through excess of impudence (al-qiḥḥa) and obstinacy (al-ʿinād)? And these promises and these good tidings that we have mentioned, together with what we shall yet mention — though they bear upon those whom we set out to refute in this bab, there is in them also a refutation of the Muslims, and of everyone who affirms a religion other than the religion of Judaism (al-yahūdiyya), which is the ordinances of the Torah — [a refutation] of anyone, [that is,] who affirms prophecy [at all].

And of the same kind as what we have mentioned is his saying, in יְשַׁעְיָה [Isa 66:19] וְשַׂמְתִּי בָהֶם אוֹת וְשִׁלַּחְתִּי מֵהֶם פְּלֵיטִים etc. ("and I will set a sign among them, and send from them survivors"). And where [stands the fulfilment of] the saying of עָמוֹס [9:13] הִנֵּה יָמִים בָּאִים נְאֻם יְיָ וְנִגַּשׁ חוֹרֵשׁ בַּקֹּצֵר וְדֹרֵךְ עֲנָבִים בְּמֹשֵׁךְ הַזָּרַע etc. ("behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when the plowman shall overtake the reaper"), [Amos 9:14] וְשַׁבְתִּי אֶת שְׁבוּת עַמִּי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבָנוּ עָרִים נְשַׁמּוֹת וְיָשָׁבוּ ("and I will turn the captivity of my people Israel, and they shall build the waste cities and inhabit them"), [Amos 9:15] וּנְטַעְתִּים עַל אַדְמָתָם וְלֹא יִנָּתְשׁוּ עוֹד etc. ("and I will plant them upon their land, and they shall no more be uprooted")? And where [stands] the saying of עוֹבַדְיָה [1:1] כֹּה אָמַר יְיָ אֱלֹהִים לֶאֱדוֹם שְׁמוּעָה שָׁמַעְנוּ מֵאֵת יְיָ etc. ("thus says the Lord God concerning Edom: we have heard a report from the Lord")? — and people, concerning that [Edom], are of two persuasions: some say they are the Romans (al-Rūm), and some say they are the Arabs (al-ʿArab). And he says, at the end of the account [Obad 1:16] כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר שְׁתִיתֶם עַל הַר קָדְשִׁי יִשְׁתּוּ כָל הַגּוֹיִם סָבִיב etc. ("for as you drank upon my holy mountain, so shall all the nations drink continually"), [Obad 1:17] וּבְהַר צִיּוֹן תִּהְיֶה פְּלֵיטָה וְהָיָה קֹדֶשׁ etc. ("and on Mount Zion there shall be deliverance, and it shall be holy"), [Obad 1:18] וְהָיָה בֵית יַעֲקֹב אֵשׁ וּבֵית יוֹסֵף לֶהָבָה וּבֵית [עֵשָׂו לְקַשׁ] ("and the house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble").

: With §8 the argument widens twice. First, the unfulfilled messianic tidings refute not only the "already-fulfilled" party but anyone who affirms prophecy yet holds a religion other than Torah-Judaism — explicitly "the Muslims and everyone who affirms a religion other than … the ordinances of the Torah." This is a striking generalizing aside: the catalogue of pending prophecies is, for Q, a standing refutation of naskh-religions as such, because the prophets they too revere foretold an unrealized Jewish redemption. Second, Q adds the Edom/Obadiah dossier (Isa 66:19; Amos 9:13-15; Obad 1:1, 16-18): the promised fire-of-Jacob consuming the stubble-of-Esau has plainly not occurred. The gloss on Edom ("some say the Romans, some say the Arabs") is Q's note on the contemporary identification of the prophetic "Edom" — the Byzantine Romans or the Arab-Muslim power — both of which still stand, hence the prophecy is pending.
§9 — Further unfulfilled tidings: Zion's saviors, the restored judges, the eschatological wonders, Gog and Magog, the temple and the healing river

[And] in [Obad 1:21] [וְעָלוּ] מוֹשִׁעִים בְּהַר צִיּוֹן לִשְׁפֹּט אֶת הַר עֵשָׂו וְהָיְתָה לַיְיָ הַמְּלוּכָה ("and saviors shall go up on Mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau, and the kingdom shall be the Lord's") and יִשְׁכֹּן וְיָרְשׁוּ הַנֶּגֶב אֶת הַר עֵשָׂו etc. And where [stands] the saying of צְפַנְיָה [3:13] שְׁאֵרִית יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יַעֲשׂוּ עַוְלָה וְלֹא יְדַבְּרוּ כָזָב etc. ("the remnant of Israel shall do no iniquity and speak no lie"), [Zeph 3:14] רָנִּי בַת צִיּוֹן הָרִיעוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל etc. ("sing, O daughter of Zion; shout, O Israel"), [Zeph 3:15] הֵסִיר יְיָ מִשְׁפָּטַיִךְ פִּנָּה אֹיְבֵךְ etc. ("the Lord has removed your judgments, he has cleared away your enemy"), to the end of the account? And when was the saying of יְשַׁעְיָהוּ [2:2] נָכוֹן יִהְיֶה הַר בֵּית יְיָ בְּרֹאשׁ הֶהָרִים etc. ("the mountain of the Lord's house shall be established at the head of the mountains") correct [i.e., fulfilled], [Isa 2:3] וְהָלְכוּ עַמִּים רַבִּים etc. ("and many peoples shall go")? In what age was his saying, in מִיכָה [7:15] כִּימֵי צֵאתְךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם אַרְאֶנּוּ נִפְלָאוֹת etc. ("as in the days when you came out of Egypt, I will show him wonders")? And his saying, in הוֹשֵׁעַ [2:16] לָכֵן הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי מְפַתֶּיהָ וְהֹלַכְתִּיהָ הַמִּדְבָּר וְדִבַּרְתִּי עַל לִבָּהּ etc. ("therefore behold, I will allure her and bring her into the wilderness and speak to her heart"), and the whole account? And who has heard that the saying in זְכַרְיָה [8:4] עֹד יֵשְׁבוּ זְקֵנִים וּזְקֵנוֹת בִּרְחֹבוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַם וְאִישׁ מִשְׁעַנְתּוֹ בְּיָדוֹ מֵרֹב יָמִים ("again shall old men and old women sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each with his staff in hand for fullness of days") had been [fulfilled]? And when was his saying in [Zech 12:4] אַכֶּה כָל סוּס בַּתִּמָּהוֹן וְרֹכְבוֹ בַּשִּׁגָּעוֹן etc. ("I will smite every horse with bewilderment and its rider with madness")? And his saying in [Zech 8:23] אֲשֶׁר יַחֲזִיקוּ עֲשָׂרָה אֲנָשִׁים מִכֹּל לְשֹׁנוֹת הַגּוֹיִם ("that ten men from all the tongues of the nations shall take hold")? And when was the affair of גּוֹג וּמָגוֹג and the marvels in it — such as [Ezek 38:20] וְרָעֲשׁוּ מִפָּנַי דְּגֵי הַיָּם וְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וְחַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה ("the fish of the sea and the birds of the heaven and the beasts of the field shall quake before me"), [Ezek 39:12] וּקְבָרוּם בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַעַן טַהֵר אֶת הָאָרֶץ ("and the house of Israel shall bury them, in order to cleanse the land"), and likewise [Ezek 39:9] וְיָצְאוּ יֹשְׁבֵי עָרֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבִעֲרוּ וְהִשִּׂיקוּ ("and the dwellers of the cities of Israel shall go out and kindle and burn") — and likewise all that follows that, of the building of the temple, and what is mentioned of the length and breadth and the magnificent vast measurements, and the affair of [Ezek 47:12] וְעַל הַנַּחַל יַעֲלֶה עַל שְׂפָתוֹ מִזֶּה וּמִזֶּה כָּל עֵץ מַאֲכָל etc. ("and by the stream, upon its bank on this side and that, shall grow every tree for food"), [Ezek 47:9] כִּי בָאוּ שָׁמָּה הַמַּיִם הָאֵלֶּה וְיֵרָפְאוּ וָחָי etc. ("for these waters come there, and [the others] are healed, and everything lives")?

: §9 piles up the wholly-unrealized eschatological tableau, each item flagged by a rhetorical "when / who has heard that…?": Obadiah's saviors judging Esau (1:21); Zephaniah's sinless remnant and the removal of Israel's judgments (3:13-15); Isaiah's mountain-of-the-Lord drawing the nations (2:2-3); the new Exodus-wonders (Mic 7:15); the wilderness-wooing (Hos 2:16); old folk safe in Jerusalem's streets (Zech 8:4); the smiting of horse and rider (Zech 12:4); ten gentiles grasping a Jew's hem (Zech 8:23); and above all the Gog-and-Magog war with its cosmic marvels, the seven-month burial and the burning of weaponry (Ezek 38–39), the dimensions of Ezekiel's visionary temple (Ezek 40–43), and the healing river issuing from it (Ezek 47:9, 12). The accumulation drives toward §10's challenge: none of this happened in the Second Temple period, so the temple Ezekiel saw is still future. The cluster ties directly back to Bab 14's "Ezekiel's temple ≠ the Second Temple."
§10 — How could anyone tally these unfulfilled tidings? The figurative escape is illegitimate

And how can the obstinate one (al-muʿṣī) presume to tally what is in Scripture of this — of that whereby their disgrace (faḍīḥa) is made plain and their obstinacy laid bare? Now they may interpret some of what we have mentioned by inner (allegorical) interpretations (taʾwīlāt bāṭina); but it is not right that any heed be paid to that from them, nor that it be heard — since interpretation and the resort to the inner sense (istiʿmāl al-bāṭin) are had recourse to only at need, and that is when the literal sense (al-ẓāhir) is such that reason renders it impossible, or it gives rise to [the appearance of] contradiction. But when no such thing occurs in it, and the literal sense neither breaks down nor turns absurd, then the obligatory thing is to hold fast to it [the literal] rather than to the inner. Moreover, that for which interpretation is feasible for them is [only] the little of what we have mentioned; as for the most of it, interpretation is not palatable for them in it — rather the corruption of the interpretation they claim for it is plain and manifest.

: Q's hermeneutical close, identical in principle to Bab 6 §1: taʾwīl (allegorical/inner reading) is a remedy of necessity only — licit when the literal sense is rationally impossible or self-contradictory, illicit when the literal sense stands sound. Since the redemption-prophecies are not rationally impossible (a future literal redemption is entirely possible), there is no warrant to allegorize them into "already-fulfilled spiritual" senses; the obligation is to the ẓāhir. And even granting that a few verses might bear a figurative reading, the bulk cannot — the sheer mass of the §§2–9 catalogue is the point: one or two verses might be explained away, but not scores of them in matched opposition. al-muʿṣī ("the obstinate/disobedient one") and faḍīḥa ("disgrace") are Q's standing polemical register (glossary §IX).
§11 — Is the messianic age the abode of reward? It belongs to this world, but is its most excellent age

Now perhaps a questioner may ask about the dominion of the Messiah and his days — whether it is an abode of reward (dār thawāb) or what it is. The answer in that is what some of the scholars have said: that the time of the Messiah is part of this present abode, since there is in it eating and drinking and procreation and plowing and planting and menstruation and impurity and death — for [Scripture] says [Isa 65:22] כִּי כִימֵי הָעֵץ [יְמֵי עַמִּי] etc. ("for as the days of a tree shall the days of my people be"), [Isa 65:20] כִּי הַנַּעַר בֶּן מֵאָה שָׁנָה יָמוּת etc. ("for the youth shall die a hundred years old") — except that it is more excellent than [the world] is now, since this abode's times may differ in degree, so that some times are more fertile and more bountiful than others, and this is observed [in experience]. Since that is so, it is admissible that the time of the Messiah and its people be more abounding in good, bounty, and fertility than all the times that preceded it; and likewise the life of its people [be] more excellent than the life of all who preceded them since the beginning of the world — just as the life of the people of the age of Adam (peace be upon him) was longer than the life of those who came after them. And there is here no indication of how great the measure of the duration of their time [will be]; and it is admissible that it be more than the measure of the duration of this [present] world in its entirety.

If it be said that that is a reward, by way of the immediate reward (al-thawāb al-ʿājil) promised in [Lev 26 — פָּרָשַׁת בְּחֻקֹּתַי] אִם בְּחֻקֹּתַי [תֵּלֵכוּ] etc., and in [Deut 11 — פָּרָשַׁת [וְהָיָה עֵקֶב]] וְהָיָה [אִם שָׁמֹעַ תִּשְׁמְעוּ] etc. — that is admissible. And if it be said that that falls within what we have related concerning the one who held that reward is of two kinds — one of them worldly (dunyāwī), attaching to the bodies, and one of them heavenly (samāwī), attaching to the souls — [namely] he who held that its measure is a hundred thousand years, which are אֶלֶף דּוֹר ("a thousand generations") — [then] that too is admissible. And God knows best.

: The doctrinal core (and the bridge to the eschatology block, glossary §VI). The question is whether the messianic age is al-dār al-ākhira (the world-to-come, the abode of thawāb) or part of this world. Q's answer, "what some of the scholars have said," is that it belongs to this abode — it has the marks of mundane life (eating, procreation, agriculture, ritual impurity, death; Isa 65:20-22's centenarian who still dies is the prooftext) — but is its supreme, most-bountiful epoch, on analogy with the longevity of Adam's generation. Its duration is unknown, possibly exceeding all prior world-history. Q then aligns this with two received frameworks: (a) the al-thawāb al-ʿājil (the "immediate"/this-worldly reward promised in the Lev 26 / Deut 11 blessing-passages), and (b) the two-tier reward doctrine (worldly thawāb to bodies, heavenly thawāb to souls) of an authority who put the messianic span at 100,000 years = elef dor ("a thousand generations," Ps 105:8 / Deut 7:9). The repeated jāʾiz ("admissible") and the closing wa-llāh aʿlam mark Q's deliberate doctrinal reserve: he reports the views as tenable without dogmatically choosing. thawāb / ʿiqāb are the anchor-terms the glossary stages for §VI.
§12 — The two classes of the redeemed: the living to whom the Messiah comes, and the revived dead

And I say also, according to what becomes apparent to me, that the nation (al-umma), in the days of the Messiah, [consists] of two remnants. The one of them: the living, to whom he comes; and the other: the dead, who come to life at his coming. So it is admissible that those who [now] live [i.e. are revived] are the ones who come to [enjoy] the Garden (al-janna) and its age — [the] חַיִּים ("living/life") — while the living to whom he comes are the ones who are with him in his dominion and his kingship, and they are the ones upon whom the good tidings and the promises fell. And concerning both classes (al-ṭāʾifatayn) together it is said [Isa 66:24] וְיָצְאוּ וְרָאוּ בְּפִגְרֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים ("and they shall go forth and look upon the corpses of the men"); and concerning all of them it is said [Exod 16:31 / Jer 8:3] וְקָנוּ שָׁם [Jer 8:3] וּבָחַר מָוֶת מֵחַיִּים … לְכֹל יְרֵאֵי שְׁמוֹ, לֹא יֵאָמֵר רְשָׁעִים ("and death shall be chosen rather than life … [but] for all who fear his name, it shall not be said [thus of the] wicked"). And this statement, even though it is [advanced] by way of [reasoned] opinion (al-raʾy), is not subject to censure, and the rational texts (al-nuṣūṣ al-ʿaqliyya) require it for whoever ponders it.

: The phrase וְקָנוּ שָׁם ("and there they shall acquire / nest") and the surrounding Hebrew at the §12 close are textually unstable in both OCR passes (the maqala3-bab24 folio gives וְקָנוּ שָׁם with a marginal "שְׁמוֹת [Exod] 16:31" that does not match the words; the maqala3-bab25 folio replaces the whole cluster with נִשְׁבַּע [יְיָ] … וְעוֹד יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ [Isa 40:31] בְּמַלְאָכִי [Mal] 3 וְזָרְחָה לָכֶם יִרְאֵי שְׁמִי [Mal 3:20] נִשְׁבַּע [יְיָ] וִיצָאתֶם וּפִשְׁתֶּם … רְשָׁעִים). The two passes disagree at the consonantal level (diff-report p161 rows 5–12), so the exact prooftext Q cited here cannot be recovered with confidence; the Isa 66:24 citation at the head of the verse-cluster is, however, secure in both passes. Reading flagged, not emended.

: Q's own tentative contribution ("according to what becomes apparent to me," ʿalā mā yalūḥu lī), explicitly framed as raʾy (considered opinion) rather than demonstrated doctrine. The redeemed nation in the messianic age comprises two ṭāʾifas: (1) the living at the Messiah's coming, who enter his earthly dominion and inherit the fulfilled "good tidings and promises" of §§2–9; and (2) the dead, resurrected at his coming, who attain the Garden (al-janna) — the everlasting "life" (ḥayyim). This neatly knits together the two foregoing strands: §§2–10's this-worldly redemption-prophecies (which fall to class 1) and the resurrection doctrine of Bab 8 (class 2). Isa 66:24 ("they shall go forth and look upon the corpses") is read as embracing both groups together. Q's closing self-defense — that an argument from raʾy is unobjectionable when "the rational texts require it" — guards the speculative move: it is offered as reasoned, not as revealed. This sentence concludes Bab 24; the הַבָּאַב הַחָאמִס וְעִשְׂרִין ("Bab 25") heading follows immediately, opening the resurrection-of-Enoch-and-Elijah bab.

- The bab's subject and adversary. The heading (reconstructed from the corrupt p166 opening, which the diff-report shows the Kraken pass mangled into gibberish) is unambiguous in sense: against whoever held that the promised (Ezekielian) temple and all the messianic-age tidings were already realized in the Second Temple and are spent. The double adversary is named at §9 (Bab 14's parallel passage): the Christians ("the Romans … uncircumcised … held Jerusalem," in Bab 14's idiom) and, primarily for this Babs-21–24 run, a Jewish party — "a people of those firm in the religion who shared with them in that," i.e. the Daniel al-Qūmisī circle whose realized-eschatology / anti-naẓar positions Q has been refuting since Bab 21. At §8 the refutation is widened to all affirmers of a non-Torah religion who nonetheless affirm prophecy — explicitly "the Muslims."

- The taqābul (matched-opposition) method (§§2–6). The bab's most distinctive feature is its long catalogue of promise-against-documented-contrary, each pair drawn so that the messianic tiding (Isaiah/Ezekiel/Jeremiah/Zechariah) is set beside an explicit Ezra-Nehemiah notice of the opposite historical condition: all-righteous people / "we have trespassed"; dominion over nations / "we are slaves this day"; gates ever-open / gates barred till noon; in-gathering from the four corners / return "from Babylon alone"; multiplication as the sand / "the people were few"; pure universal speech / children "cannot speak Judahite"; no oppressor + native ruler / "the governors laid heavy burdens"; harvest never feeding enemies / "its increase to the kings set over us." The argument is internal-consistency: Scripture cannot simultaneously promise X for the redemption and record not-X for the Second-Temple period unless the redemption is still future.

- From "promise vs. past contrary" to "promise vs. never-occurred" (§§7–9). At §7 Q shifts register: the conquering Messiah of Isa 11:4 fits neither Jesus (killed) nor the failed Jewish messianic claimants Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī and Yūdghān — a notable moment where Q lines up Christian and intra-Jewish false-messiahs as joint counter-examples (cross-referring to his own sect-catalogue in Maqala I). §§8–9 then heap up the wholly unrealized tableau — Edom's destruction (Obadiah), the new-Exodus wonders, Gog-and-Magog, Ezekiel's temple and healing river — none of which the Second Temple era saw.

- The hermeneutical control (§10). taʾwīl / al-bāṭin (allegory) is a remedy of necessity, licit only where the literal sense is rationally impossible or contradictory; since a future literal redemption is perfectly possible, allegorizing the prophecies into "already-fulfilled spiritual" senses is illegitimate. And the mass of the catalogue is itself an argument: a handful of verses might be explained away, the bulk cannot. This is the same taʾwīl-as-farʿ-of-aṣl posture of Bab 6 §1, here turned against realized eschatology.

- The messianic age as the supreme epoch of this world (§11). Against any reading of the messianic age as the dār al-ākhira, Q (reporting "some of the scholars") locates it within this abode — it retains eating, procreation, agriculture, ritual impurity, and death (Isa 65:20's centenarian who dies) — while being the most bountiful and long-lived epoch ever, on the Adam-longevity analogy. He aligns this non-committally with both the al-thawāb al-ʿājil (this-worldly reward of the Lev 26 / Deut 11 blessings) and a two-tier (bodily/worldly + spiritual/heavenly) reward scheme that fixed the span at 100,000 years = elef dor. The studied jāʾiz … wa-llāh aʿlam reserve is characteristic.

- The two remnants and the bridge to resurrection (§12). Q's own raʾy: the messianic nation = the living (who enter the Messiah's earthly dominion and inherit §§2–9's tidings) + the resurrected dead (who attain the Garden / everlasting ḥayyim). This unites the bab's this-worldly redemption-prophecies with the resurrection doctrine argued in Bab 8, and is offered as reasoned opinion that "the rational texts require." The bab closes here; Bab 25 ("that Enoch and Elijah did not ascend bodily") follows immediately — and §12's resurrection-and-ascent themes set it up.

- Text-critical note on the citations. The seven folios (p166→p160) carried an exceptionally high OCR disagreement rate (295 Hebrew runs flagged in the diff-report), because the bab is almost wholly a chain of densely packed biblical citations with marginal sigla. The multimodal pass is markedly superior to Kraken (which produced near-gibberish for most verses); citations above follow the multimodal reading, silently corrected to the Masoretic text where the consonantal skeleton was secure, and the marginal book-and-chapter pointers (often abbreviated בשם = "in the same [book]") normalized to standard references. The one genuinely unrecoverable spot is the §12 closing prooftext-cluster, where the two passes disagree at the consonantal level (see ); it is flagged, not emended.
